pos: adj. (conformable to fact; also genuine, real, as opposed to the shadow; rendering Hebrew emet, Greek alethes, alethinos)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon treowe, faithful, trusty — the same root as trust and troth. The English word begins with fidelity, not with accuracy, and so does the Hebrew.
biblical_def: True in Scripture carries two senses that must be kept together. The first is factual: Deuteronomy requires that a capital charge be examined until “it be true, and the thing certain” (Deu 17:4). Joseph's brothers plead it of themselves — “we are true men, thy servants are no spies” (Gen 42:11) — where true means honest, not merely accurate. Boaz uses it of a legal fact he cannot evade: “it is true that I am thy near kinsman: howbeit there is a kinsman nearer than I” (Rut 3:12). The second sense is the Greek alethinos: not the opposite of false but the opposite of the shadow, the real as against the copy. So the Lord Jesus says, “I am the true vine” (John 15:1) — Israel was a vine, and He is the reality it pictured. Both senses meet in Philippians 4:8, where Paul makes truth the first filter of Christian thought: “whatsoever things are true… think on these things”.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines true as conformable to fact, not false, and also as genuine, pure, real, not counterfeit — and as faithful, steady in adhering to friends, to promises, or to a prince.
webster_full: TRUE, a. Conformable to fact; being in accordance with the actual state of things; as a true relation.
2. Genuine; pure; real; not counterfeit, adulterated or false; as true balsam.
3. Faithful; steady in adhering to friends, to promises, to a prince, or to the state; loyal.
4. Honest; not fraudulent. We are true men; thy servants are no spies. Gen. xlii.
scriptures: John 15:1
I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.
Php 4:8

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
Deu 17:4
And it be told thee, and thou hast heard of it, and enquired diligently, and, behold, it be true, and the thing certain, that such abomination is wrought in Israel:
Rut 3:12
And now it is true that I am thy near kinsman: howbeit there is a kinsman nearer than I.
corruption_summary: Truth relocated from correspondence with reality to sincerity or perspective — my truth — which makes the word unusable for the one thing Scripture uses it for.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant move of the age is to make truth a possession rather than a property: a thing is true for someone, and the honest expression of a conviction becomes indistinguishable from its accuracy. Deuteronomy 17:4 forecloses that immediately — a charge must be enquired into diligently until it is true, and the thing certain, because a man's life turns on the difference between a sincere accusation and an accurate one. Wherever the distinction collapses, the vulnerable are the first to suffer.

The deeper loss is the second sense. Alethinos means real as against the shadow, and it is the word by which the New Testament claims that the Old Testament's furniture was always a picture: the true vine, the true light, the true tabernacle, the true bread from heaven. That vocabulary is how Scripture teaches the believer to read the Old Testament without either discarding it or freezing in it. And Philippians 4:8 makes the whole matter practical: what is true is the first thing a Christian mind is commanded to dwell upon.
roots_summary: Hebrew emet (H571), truth, firmness, faithfulness — from aman, to support, the root of amen; Greek alethes (G227), not concealed, true; alethinos (G228), real, genuine, as opposed to the shadow.
roots_lines: Hebrew emet (H571) — truth, firmness; built on aman, to be firm, from which amen comes — truth as what holds weight.
Greek alethes (G227) — true, unconcealed; the opposite of falsehood, as in Php 4:8.
Greek alethinos (G228) — genuine, real, the substance rather than the shadow; the true vine (John 15:1), the true light, the true tabernacle (Heb 8:2).
usage: “I am the true vine” — not merely truthful; the reality the shadow pictured.
“Whatsoever things are true… think on these things” — the first filter of Christian thought.
“It be true, and the thing certain” — sincerity is not the same as accuracy.

pos: v. (to exercise the mind, judge, purpose; rendering Hebrew chashab, zakar, Greek logizomai, phroneo)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon thencan, closely joined to thancian, to thank — thinking and thanking share a root, and Scripture keeps them close.
biblical_def: Think in the Authorized Version usually means to reckon or to purpose, not merely to have a passing notion. Joseph asks the butler, “think on me when it shall be well with thee” (Gen 40:14) — remember me, act on it. Nehemiah's repeated prayer is the same word turned Godward: “Think upon me, my God, for good” (Neh 5:19), and against his enemies, “think thou upon Tobiah and Sanballat according to these their works” (Neh 6:14). It also names presumption: Abijah rebukes the northern kingdom — “ye think to withstand the kingdom of the LORD” (2Ch 13:8) — a plan, not a musing. And Mordecai uses it for the fatal self-deception of the sheltered: “Think not with thyself that thou shalt escape in the king's house, more than all the Jews” (Est 4:13). Paul then gives the Christian mind its standing curriculum in Philippians 4:8, ending with the imperative that governs the whole list — think on these things.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines think as to have the mind occupied on some subject, to judge, to conclude, to determine — and to intend or mean, as in he thinks to deceive us.
webster_full: THINK, v.i. To have the mind occupied on some subject; to have ideas, or to revolve ideas in the mind.
2. To judge; to conclude; to hold as a settled opinion.
3. To intend; to mean.
Let him that thinketh he standeth, take heed lest he fall. 1 Cor. x.
scriptures: Php 4:8

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
Est 4:13
Then Mordecai commanded to answer Esther, Think not with thyself that thou shalt escape in the king's house, more than all the Jews.
Neh 5:19
Think upon me, my God, for good, according to all that I have done for this people.
And now ye think to withstand the kingdom of the LORD in the hand of the sons of David; and ye be a great multitude, and there are with you golden calves, which Jeroboam made you for gods.
corruption_summary: The mind treated as a passive receiver of whatever passes through it, and thought as involuntary — where Scripture commands a curriculum and holds a man responsible for what he dwells upon.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern assumption is that thoughts happen to a man and only actions are his. Philippians 4:8 is an imperative: think on these things, with an itemized list of what qualifies. That presupposes the mind can be directed — not that stray thoughts can be prevented, but that what a man dwells on is a matter of obedience. In an economy engineered to occupy attention continuously, this command has become both harder and more urgent, and it cannot be obeyed passively.

Esther 4:13 supplies the sharpest warning to the comfortable, and it is the same verb. Mordecai does not tell Esther she is obliged to act because she is powerful; he tells her not to think with herself that the palace will save her. Self-deception is a species of thinking, done privately and plausibly, and it flourishes exactly where a person has enough shelter to make it seem reasonable. The remedy Mordecai offers is not a better feeling but a truer reckoning: deliverance will arise elsewhere, and who knows whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this.
roots_summary: Hebrew chashab (H2803), to reckon, devise, impute; zakar (H2142), to remember — the word behind think on me; Greek logizomai (G3049), to reckon, and phroneo (G5426), to set the mind.
roots_lines: Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to think, reckon, devise; the same verb used when righteousness was counted to Abraham (Gen 15:6).
Hebrew zakar (H2142) — to remember; Nehemiah's think upon me, my God is a plea for remembrance, not attention (Neh 5:19).
Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, take account of; the imperative in Php 4:8, a bookkeeping word applied to the mind.
usage: “Think on these things” — a commanded curriculum for the mind.
“Think not with thyself that thou shalt escape” — self-deception is a kind of thinking.
“Think upon me, my God, for good” — a plea for remembrance.

pos: adj. (at liberty, not in bondage; also given without price; rendering Hebrew chophshi, nedabah, Greek eleutheros, dorean)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon freo, related to words for love and friendship — the free man was originally the beloved member of the household, not the outsider.
biblical_def: Free in Scripture is release granted rather than seized. Exodus 21 governs it: a Hebrew servant serves six years, “and in the seventh he shall go out free for nothing” (Exo 21:2) — freedom by calendar, not by revolt. A master who destroys a servant's eye or knocks out a tooth must “let him go free” (Exo 21:26) — the servant's body is protected by a law the master cannot overrule. Deuteronomy adds that he must not be sent away empty (Deu 15:13). Most striking is the servant who refuses release: “I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free” (Exo 21:5) — bondage chosen out of love, the ear bored at the doorpost, which the New Testament takes up when Paul calls himself the bondservant of Christ. And the Lord Jesus locates real freedom in an unexpected place: “ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free” (John 8:32).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines free as being at liberty, not being under necessity or restraint, physical or moral — and also as gratuitous, not gained by importunity or purchase.
webster_full: FREE, a. Being at liberty; not being under necessity or restraint, physical or moral.
2. In government, not enslaved; not in a state of vassalage or dependence.
3. Instituted by a free people, or by consent or choice of those who are to be subjects.
4. Open; candid; frank; ingenuous. 5. Gratuitous; not gained by importunity or purchase; as a free gift.
scriptures: John 8:32
And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.
Exo 21:2
If thou buy an Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve: and in the seventh he shall go out free for nothing.
Exo 21:5
And if the servant shall plainly say, I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free:
And if a man smite the eye of his servant, or the eye of his maid, that it perish; he shall let him go free for his eye's sake.
corruption_summary: Freedom redefined as the absence of all constraint and the sovereignty of the self — where Scripture presents it as release into a rightful service, and shows a man choosing bondage out of love.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning definition of freedom is negative: fewer limits, more options, no authority above the self. Scripture's freedom is directional. Israel is brought out of Egypt in order to serve the LORD, and the demand to Pharaoh is never let my people go full stop, but let my people go, that they may serve me. Freedom in that grammar is not the absence of a master but deliverance from a cruel one into a good one, which is why John 8:32 can locate liberty in knowing the truth rather than in the removal of a constraint.

Exodus 21:5 is the passage that dismantles the modern definition entirely. A man legally entitled to walk away says, I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free, and has his ear bored to the doorpost. By any autonomous account this is the surrender of freedom; by the Bible's account it is its highest exercise, and it becomes the model for every apostle who opens a letter by calling himself a bondservant of Jesus Christ. The freest men in Scripture are the ones most thoroughly owned.
roots_summary: Hebrew chophshi (H2670), free, released from bondage; nedabah (H5071), a freewill offering; Greek eleutheros (G1658), free; dorean (G1432), freely, as a gift.
roots_lines: Hebrew chophshi (H2670) — free, at liberty; the seventh-year release of the Hebrew servant (Exo 21:2).
Hebrew nedabah (H5071) — a voluntary or freewill offering; the free offerings brought every morning for the sanctuary (Exo 36:3).
Greek eleutheros (G1658) — free, unrestrained; if the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed (John 8:36).
usage: “The truth shall make you free” — liberty located in knowing, not in the removal of limits.
“In the seventh he shall go out free for nothing” — release by calendar, not revolt.
“I love my master… I will not go out free” — the freest man in the chapter.

pos: adj. (heavy, burdensome, causing grief; rendering Hebrew kabed, ra, Greek barus)
etymology: From Old French grief, heavy, from Latin gravis, weighty. The Hebrew word most often behind it, kabed, likewise means heavy — and is the same root as glory.
biblical_def: Grievous means heavy, and Scripture applies the weight in three directions. To circumstances: “the famine was grievous in the land” (Gen 12:10); a grievous swarm of flies (Exo 8:24); a very grievous murrain on the cattle (Exo 9:3). To sin, in the sentence that precedes the destruction of the cities of the plain: “because the cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and because their sin is very grievous” (Gen 18:20) — sin with weight, sin that cries. And to the affections of a good man asked to do a hard thing: “the thing was very grievous in Abraham's sight because of his son” (Gen 21:11), where God does not deny the grief but overrules it — let it not be grievous in thy sight… for in Isaac shall thy seed be called (Gen 21:12). Against all this weight stands one apostolic sentence: “his commandments are not grievous” (1Jn 5:3). Sin is heavy; obedience is not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grievous as heavy, oppressive, burdensome, and also as afflictive, painful, hard to be borne — and as atrocious, aggravated, when applied to sin.
webster_full: GRIEV´OUS, a. Heavy; oppressive; burdensome; as a grievous load of taxes.
2. Afflictive; painful; hard to be borne.
3. Causing grief or sorrow.
4. Atrocious; aggravated; as a grievous sin. Their sin is very grievous. Gen. xviii.
scriptures: For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments: and his commandments are not grievous.
And the LORD said, Because the cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and because their sin is very grievous;
And the thing was very grievous in Abraham's sight because of his son.
And there was a famine in the land: and Abram went down into Egypt to sojourn there; for the famine was grievous in the land.
corruption_summary: God's commandments felt as a weight and His grace as a relief from them — the exact reverse of 1 John 5:3, and the reason legalism and licence are both so tiring.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 John 5:3 is a claim most Christians would hesitate to make aloud: his commandments are not grievous. Not merely worth the burden — not a burden. That is unintelligible to the legalist, for whom the commandments are precisely the weight, and to the antinomian, who assumes freedom means relief from them. John locates the difference in the clause before: this is the love of God, that we keep His commandments. Commands from a Person one loves do not weigh the same as commands from a taskmaster, which is why the same law is grievous to a slave and light to a son.

Genesis 21:11 keeps this from becoming glib. Abraham was asked to send away his son, and the text says plainly it was very grievous in Abraham's sight. God does not tell him it should not have been; He tells him to hearken anyway, and attaches a promise. Obedience is not grievous in the sense John means, and it can still cost a man everything he wanted. The weight the believer is spared is the weight of sin, whose cry Genesis 18:20 says reaches heaven — not the weight of a hard providence.
roots_summary: Hebrew kabed (H3515), heavy, weighty, burdensome — the same root as kabod, glory; ra (H7451), evil, bad; Greek barus (G926), heavy — John's word denied of the commandments.
roots_lines: Hebrew kabed (H3515) — heavy, grievous; from the root that also gives kabod, glory — weight is either a burden or a splendour.
Hebrew ra (H7451) — evil, distress; the grievous plagues and famines of Genesis and Exodus.
Greek barus (G926) — heavy, weighty, burdensome; the Pharisees bind heavy burdens (Mat 23:4), and His commandments are not barus (1Jn 5:3).
usage: “His commandments are not grievous” — the same law, light to a son.
“Their sin is very grievous” — sin with weight, sin that cries.
“The thing was very grievous in Abraham's sight” — and he was told to hearken anyway.

pos: adj. and v. (containing nothing, void; rendering Hebrew req, reyqam, Greek kenos)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon aemtig, at leisure, unoccupied. Scripture uses emptiness both as a plight and as a promise — no one is to leave God's presence, or God's people's service, empty.
biblical_def: Empty is a word about hands. God's standing rule for worship is that no one comes with nothing: “none shall appear before me empty” (Exo 23:15; Exo 34:20). And His standing rule for release is that no one leaves with nothing: “when thou sendest him out free from thee, thou shalt not let him go away empty” (Deu 15:13). Even the exodus obeys it — “when ye go, ye shall not go empty” (Exo 3:21) — slaves leaving four centuries of unpaid labour with wages at last. Jacob measures Laban's injustice by the same word: but for God, “surely thou hadst sent me away now empty” (Gen 31:42). And the emptiest place in Genesis is the pit into which Joseph was cast: “the pit was empty, there was no water in it” (Gen 37:24) — a detail supplied so the reader knows he did not drown, and so the brothers could sit down to eat beside it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines empty as containing nothing, or nothing but air — and figuratively as destitute of solid matter, of sense, or of substance; vain; unsatisfactory.
webster_full: EMP´TY, a. Containing nothing, or nothing but air; as an empty chest; empty space.
2. Devoid; destitute; as a mind empty of good.
3. Destitute of solid matter, of sense, of knowledge; as empty words; an empty coxcomb.
4. Unfurnished; unsupplied; as an empty house. 5. Void; vacant.
scriptures: Thou shalt keep the feast of unleavened bread: (thou shalt eat unleavened bread seven days, as I commanded thee, in the time appointed of the month Abib; for in it thou camest out from Egypt: and none shall appear before me empty:)
And when thou sendest him out free from thee, thou shalt not let him go away empty:
Exo 3:21
And I will give this people favour in the sight of the Egyptians: and it shall come to pass, that, when ye go, ye shall not go empty:
And they took him, and cast him into a pit: and the pit was empty, there was no water in it.
corruption_summary: Worship approached empty-handed as a matter of course, and workers released empty as a matter of contract — both against a law that requires the hands to be full in either direction.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The neglected law is symmetrical and worth restoring in both halves. Godward: none shall appear before me empty. The New Testament does not repeat the specific offerings, and it nowhere reverses the instinct — a worship in which nothing is brought, given, or offered has lost something the feasts of Israel took for granted. Manward: thou shalt not let him go away empty. A servant leaving in the seventh year was to be furnished liberally out of the flock, the floor, and the winepress, which is a standard of severance no employment contract requires and every Christian employer should feel.

The principle joining the two is that God fills empty hands and expects His people to do the same. Exodus 3:21 is the clearest case: a nation of slaves with four hundred years of unpaid labour behind them does not leave empty, and the wages come from the very people who withheld them. Genesis 37:24 supplies the counter-image of hardness — the pit was empty, and the brothers sat down to eat bread beside it.
roots_summary: Hebrew req (H7386), empty, vain, worthless; reyqam (H7387), emptily, without cause; Greek kenos (G2756), empty, hollow — the root of the verb Paul uses of Christ emptying Himself.
roots_lines: Hebrew req (H7386) — empty, vain; the empty pit of Gen 37:24 and the empty ears of Pharaoh's dream (Gen 41:27).
Hebrew reyqam (H7387) — empty-handed, without cause; the standing word in none shall appear before me empty (Exo 23:15).
Greek kenoo (G2758) — to empty, make void; made himself of no reputation (Php 2:7) is literally emptied himself.
usage: “None shall appear before me empty” — hands full toward God.
“Thou shalt not let him go away empty” — hands full toward the departing servant.
“The pit was empty, there was no water in it” — and they sat down to eat bread.

pos: adj. (refusing subjection to lawful authority; rendering Hebrew marah, meri, sarar)
etymology: From Latin rebellis, from re- and bellum, war — to renew war against a power one has already been subject to. Rebellion presupposes a prior allegiance.
biblical_def: Rebellious is Scripture's verdict on a covenant people, not on outsiders, and the etymology explains why: one can only rebel where one already owed allegiance. Moses makes it the summary of an entire generation: “Ye have been rebellious against the LORD from the day that I knew you” (Deu 9:24), and he expects no improvement after his death (Deu 31:27). The household law of Deuteronomy 21 names the same disposition in a son: “This our son is stubborn and rebellious, he will not obey our voice; he is a glutton, and a drunkard” (Deu 21:20) — brought by both parents to the elders, a public process with the family as accuser rather than a private power. Saul, in his rage, throws the word at his own son as an insult (1Sa 20:30). And Ezra records that Jerusalem itself had a reputation abroad as “a rebellious city, and hurtful unto kings” (Ezr 4:15) — the accusation of enemies, and not entirely a lie.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rebellious as engaged in rebellion, renouncing the authority and dominion of the government to which allegiance is due — and as refractory or refusing due subjection.
webster_full: REBEL´LIOUS, a. Engaged in rebellion; renouncing the authority and dominion of the government to which obedience is due.
2. In Scripture, refusing due subjection to God; disobedient.
Rebellious children. Is. xxx.
3. Refractory; obstinate; as a rebellious son.
scriptures: Deu 9:24
Ye have been rebellious against the LORD from the day that I knew you.
And they shall say unto the elders of his city, This our son is stubborn and rebellious, he will not obey our voice; he is a glutton, and a drunkard.
For I know thy rebellion, and thy stiff neck: behold, while I am yet alive with you this day, ye have been rebellious against the LORD; and how much more after my death?
Ezr 4:15

That search may be made in the book of the records of thy fathers: so shalt thou find in the book of the records, and know that this city is a rebellious city, and hurtful unto kings and provinces, and that they have moved sedition within the same of old time: for which cause was this city destroyed. moved: Cald.
corruption_summary: Rebellion romanticized — the rebel as the honest one, authority as the thing that must always be resisted — while Scripture ranks it beside witchcraft.
corruption_paragraphs: A long strand of modern storytelling makes the rebel the hero by definition, and its influence on Christians is easy to underestimate. Scripture's estimate is different: rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness as iniquity and idolatry. The reason is structural. Rebellion is not merely disobedience but the renunciation of a relationship in which obedience was owed, which is why Deuteronomy 9:24 can characterize a whole generation by it and why Moses expects it to outlive him.

Deuteronomy 21:18-21 must be handled with care, and its details resist the caricature. The parents bring the charge together, to the elders of the city, publicly — the father cannot act as judge in his own house. The son is grown, and the charge is settled character, not childish disobedience. The passage removes power from the paterfamilias and gives it to a court, which was a restraint on ancient household authority rather than a licence for it. And it stands in the canon as the measure of how seriously God takes the first authority a person ever knows.
roots_summary: Hebrew marah (H4784), to be contentious, rebel; meri (H4805), rebellion — Ezekiel's rebellious house; sarar (H5637), to be stubborn, turn away.
roots_lines: Hebrew marah (H4784) — to rebel, be disobedient; Moses' verdict on the wilderness generation (Deu 9:24).
Hebrew meri (H4805) — rebellion; Ezekiel is repeatedly sent to a rebellious house (Eze 2:5), and told to speak whether they hear or forbear.
Hebrew sarar (H5637) — to be stubborn, refractory; paired with rebellious in the case of the son (Deu 21:20).
usage: “Ye have been rebellious against the LORD from the day that I knew you” — a generation summarized.
“Stubborn and rebellious, he will not obey our voice” — brought by both parents to the elders.
“This city is a rebellious city” — the enemies' charge, and not entirely a lie.

pos: adj. (fair to look upon, excellent of its kind; rendering Hebrew tob, chemdah, hadar)
etymology: From good with the suffix -ly, likeness — goodly means good-looking in the old, unironic sense: a thing whose appearance answers to its quality.
biblical_def: Goodly means fair and excellent of its kind, and Scripture uses it with a careful ambivalence. It marks God's providence in the preservation of a deliverer: Moses' mother “saw him that he was a goodly child” and hid him three months (Exo 2:2) — the observation that saved Israel. It marks the beauty of the covenant people seen from outside, in the mouth of a prophet hired to curse them: “How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, and thy tabernacles, O Israel!” (Num 24:5). It marks appointed liturgical beauty — “the boughs of goodly trees, branches of palm trees” for the feast of tabernacles (Lev 23:40). But it also marks the instrument of deception: “Rebekah took goodly raiment of her eldest son Esau… and put them upon Jacob” (Gen 27:15). Goodly appearance can clothe a lie, and Scripture's recurring warning is that a goodly outside settles nothing — Joseph was a goodly person, and so was Saul.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines goodly as being of a handsome form, beautiful, graceful — and also as pleasant, agreeable, or bulky and swelling, in the sense of considerable.
webster_full: GOOD´LY, a. Being of a handsome form; beautiful; graceful; as a goodly person; goodly raiment; goodly houses.
2. Pleasant; agreeable; desirable; as goodly days.
3. Bulky; swelling; affectedly turgid.
GOOD´LY, adv. Excellently.
scriptures: Num 24:5
How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, and thy tabernacles, O Israel!
Exo 2:2
And the woman conceived, and bare a son: and when she saw him that he was a goodly child, she hid him three months.
And Rebekah took goodly raiment of her eldest son Esau, which were with her in the house, and put them upon Jacob her younger son:

And ye shall take you on the first day the boughs of goodly trees, branches of palm trees, and the boughs of thick trees, and willows of the brook; and ye shall rejoice before the LORD your God seven days.
corruption_summary: Appearance trusted as evidence of substance — a goodly outside taken for a good inside — which Genesis 27 shows to be precisely how deception works.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 27:15 is the caution this entry exists to give. Rebekah dresses Jacob in Esau's goodly raiment, and a blind father is deceived by what he can feel and smell. Goodly appearance is not evidence; it is the material out of which impostures are made. An image-driven culture has multiplied the raw material enormously, and its chief effect on the church is that leaders are selected, and movements trusted, on exactly the grounds Genesis 27 shows to be unreliable.

But the word must not be soured, because Scripture uses it gladly. Balaam, hired to curse, looked down on the tents of Israel and could only say how goodly. Moses' mother saw a goodly child and hid him, and God used that maternal observation to preserve a deliverer. The feast of tabernacles was celebrated with the boughs of goodly trees, by God's own command. Beauty is real, it is often God-given, and it settles nothing about the heart — both halves of that sentence are needed.
roots_summary: Hebrew tob (H2896), good, pleasant, fair — the goodly child of Exo 2:2; hadar (H1926), splendour, ornament — the goodly trees of the feast; chemdah (H2532), desirable, precious.
roots_lines: Hebrew tob (H2896) — good, fair, pleasing; the goodly child (Exo 2:2), the same word God speaks over creation.
Hebrew hadar (H1926) — splendour, majesty, ornament; the boughs of goodly trees commanded for tabernacles (Lev 23:40).
Hebrew chamad (H2530) — to desire, covet; the root behind goodly where the sense is desirable, and the verb of the tenth commandment.
usage: “How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob” — from the mouth of a prophet hired to curse.
“She saw him that he was a goodly child” — the observation that preserved a deliverer.
“Goodly raiment… put them upon Jacob” — the material of an imposture.

pos: adj. (worthy of honour, held in esteem; rendering Hebrew kabed, nikbad, Greek entimos, timios)
etymology: From Latin honorabilis, from honor. The Hebrew is kabed, heavy — an honourable man is a man of weight, whose word carries.
biblical_def: Honourable in Scripture means weighty, and the Hebrew idiom makes the metaphor plain: to honour is to make heavy, and to despise is to make light. Ahimelech commends David to Saul in these terms: “who is so faithful among all thy servants as David… and is honourable in thine house?” (1Sa 22:14). Samuel is introduced to Saul's servant as “an honourable man; all that he saith cometh surely to pass” (1Sa 9:6) — honour resting on the reliability of his word, which is the truest ground of it. David's mighty men are ranked by it: “He was more honourable than the thirty, but he attained not to the first three” (2Sa 23:23). And the most instructive use is Naaman: “a great man with his master, and honourable… he was also a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper” (2Ki 5:1). Four clauses of honour, and one word that undoes them all. Honour cannot reach what a man most needs cured.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines honourable as worthy of honour, illustrious, noble, and also as conferring honour, or consistent with honour and reputation — and as performed with marks of honour.
webster_full: HON´ORABLE, a. Holding a distinguished rank in society; illustrious or noble.
2. Possessing a high mind; actuated by principles of honor, or a nice sense of right and wrong.
3. Conferring honor.
4. Consistent with honor or reputation. 5. Honored; esteemed; regarded with respect.
scriptures: Now Naaman, captain of the host of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honourable, because by him the LORD had given deliverance unto Syria: he was also a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper.

And he said unto him, Behold now, there is in this city a man of God, and he is an honourable man; all that he saith cometh surely to pass: now let us go thither; peradventure he can shew us our way that we should go.
Then Ahimelech answered the king, and said, And who is so faithful among all thy servants as David, which is the king's son in law, and goeth at thy bidding, and is honourable in thine house?
He was more honourable than the thirty, but he attained not to the first three. And David set him over his guard.
corruption_summary: Reputation mistaken for honour — standing managed and purchased rather than earned by a word that holds — while the one thing a man most needs cured goes unaddressed behind it.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Kings 5:1 is one of the most efficient sentences in Scripture. Naaman is great, honourable, victorious, a mighty man in valour — and then five words: but he was a leper. Every honour he holds is genuine and none of it reaches the thing that will kill him, and the cure comes through a captive Israelite servant girl and a prophet who does not come outside to meet him. The whole narrative is an assault on honour as a category of self-assessment, and Naaman's rage at being told to wash in Jordan is precisely the rage of an honourable man asked to be treated like anyone else.

1 Samuel 9:6 supplies the positive ground the age has lost. Samuel is honourable because all that he saith cometh surely to pass — honour resting on a word that holds. Where reputation is a managed asset, built by presentation and defended by publicists, the connection between honour and reliability is severed, and the word becomes a description of standing rather than of substance. Recovering the Hebrew sense would settle much: an honourable man is one whose word is heavy enough to build on.
roots_summary: Hebrew kabed (H3513), to be heavy, and so to be honoured — the same root as glory; nikbad, the honoured or weighty one; Greek entimos (G1784), held in honour, precious.
roots_lines: Hebrew kabed (H3513) — to be heavy, honoured; the fifth commandment's honour thy father is literally make heavy.
Hebrew qalal (H7043) — to be light, and hence to curse or despise; the exact antonym, so that contempt is making light of a person.
Greek entimos (G1784) — held in honour, precious; used of the centurion's servant (Luk 7:2) and of the chief corner stone (1Pe 2:6).
usage: “A great man… and honourable… but he was a leper” — four honours, undone by one word.
“An honourable man; all that he saith cometh surely to pass” — honour resting on a reliable word.
“More honourable than the thirty, but he attained not to the first three”.

pos: adj. and n. (old, of former times; also an elder; rendering Hebrew qedem, zaqen, olam)
etymology: From Latin ante, before, through Old French ancien. In the Authorized Version the ancients often means simply the elders — age and office in one word.
biblical_def: Ancient in the Authorized Version means both old in time and old in office. Job states the general presumption: “With the ancient is wisdom; and in length of days understanding” (Job 12:12) — a presumption, not an absolute, since Elihu will shortly qualify it. Proverbs turns antiquity into a property law with wide application: “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28) — boundary stones, quietly moved at night, being the classic theft from a neighbour who cannot prove it. Ezra records the ancient men who had seen the first house weeping at the foundation of the second (Ezr 3:12), grief and shouting mingled so that no one could distinguish them. And the word rises to its height in Daniel's vision of “the Ancient of days… whose garment was white as snow” (Dan 7:9), before whom one like the Son of man is brought — the eternal God pictured in the dignity of great age.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ancient as old, that happened or existed in former times, usually at a great distance of time — and as a noun, those who lived in former ages, and also an elder or senior.
webster_full: AN´CIENT, a. Old; that happened or existed in former times, usually at a great distance of time.
2. Old; that has been of long duration; as an ancient forest.
3. Known from ancient times; as the ancient continent.
AN´CIENT, n. Generally used in the plural, ancients. Those who lived in former ages. 2. An elder or senior.
scriptures: Dan 7:9

I beheld till the thrones were cast down, and the Ancient of days did sit, whose garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head like the pure wool: his throne was like the fiery flame, and his wheels as burning fire.
Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.
With the ancient is wisdom; and in length of days understanding.
Ezr 3:12

But many of the priests and Levites and chief of the fathers, who were ancient men, that had seen the first house, when the foundation of this house was laid before their eyes, wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy:
corruption_summary: Antiquity treated as disqualification — chronological snobbery, in which a doctrine is answered by naming its age — and the landmarks quietly moved by a generation that did not set them.
corruption_paragraphs: The characteristic prejudice of the age is that later is truer. It is rarely argued, because it is rarely stated; it operates as an atmosphere in which an old confession can be dismissed by dating it. Proverbs 22:28 addresses the practice in its concrete form: remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set. Boundary stones were moved at night, a few feet at a time, by men who could always claim they had always stood there. Doctrinal landmarks move the same way, incrementally and deniably, and the generation that moves them is never the one that set them.

The safeguard against mere traditionalism is in the same Scripture. Job 12:12 is a presumption in favour of age, and Elihu — a young man — answers it directly: great men are not always wise, neither do the aged understand judgment. Antiquity is a strong witness and not the final authority; that place belongs to Scripture alone, which is why the Reformation could appeal to the most ancient thing of all against a merely old tradition. And Daniel 7:9 sets the whole matter in its proper light: only One is genuinely ancient, and the Son of man is brought before Him.
roots_summary: Hebrew qedem (H6924), the east, aforetime, ancient days; zaqen (H2205), old, an elder; attiq yomin (Aramaic), Ancient of days — Daniel's title for God.
roots_lines: Hebrew qedem (H6924) — front, east, aforetime; the eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms uses the related sense of primordial antiquity (Deu 33:27).
Hebrew zaqen (H2205) — old, aged, an elder; the ancient men who had seen the first house (Ezr 3:12).
Aramaic attiq yomin — Ancient of days; Daniel's title for the enthroned God, used three times in one chapter (Dan 7:9, 13, 22).
usage: “The Ancient of days did sit, whose garment was white as snow” — eternity pictured as great age.
“Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” — the stones move at night.
“With the ancient is wisdom” — a strong presumption, and not the final authority.

pos: v. (to test, try, put to the proof; and thereby to establish; rendering Hebrew nasah, bachan, Greek dokimazo)
etymology: From Latin probare, to test, to find good — the root of probe, probation, and approve. To prove a thing is to put it to trial; approval is the outcome, not the method.
biblical_def: Prove means to test, and Scripture is unembarrassed that God does it. “God did tempt Abraham” (Gen 22:1) — the older English tempt meaning to prove, not to entice, since God tempts no man to evil. The testing is real and its purpose is disclosure: to show what was there. Malachi contains the one place God invites men to test Him: “prove me now herewith… if I will not open you the windows of heaven” (Mal 3:10). Paul then makes proving the ordinary work of a renewed mind: “be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God” (Rom 12:2) — the will of God discerned by a mind being remade, not by a technique. He turns the same verb inward: “Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves” (2Co 13:5). And Thessalonians gives the standing rule for everything a Christian hears: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prove as to try, to ascertain some unknown quality by experiment — and then to evince, establish or ascertain as truth by testimony or argument.
webster_full: PROVE, v.t. To try; to ascertain some unknown quality or excellence by experiment or test.
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 Thess. v.
2. To evince, establish or ascertain as truth, reality or fact, by testimony or other evidence.
3. To try; to examine. Examine yourselves; prove your own selves. 2 Cor. xiii.
scriptures: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
Rom 12:2
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?
Mal 3:10

Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.
corruption_summary: Discernment outsourced — teaching received on the strength of a platform rather than proved — and self-examination replaced by self-esteem, which cannot test anything.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Thessalonians 5:21 is addressed to ordinary believers, not to specialists: prove all things. It presupposes that a Christian both may and must test what he is taught, which is the practical form of the Reformation's recovery of the open Bible. Where teaching is received on the credit of a personality, a platform, or a following, that command is not being obeyed, and the Bereans stand as the standing rebuke — they searched the Scriptures daily to see whether the apostle himself was telling the truth, and Luke calls them noble for it.

The inward use is the harder one. Prove your own selves (2Co 13:5) is not morbid introspection, which merely consults the deceiver again, but a test against an external standard: whether Jesus Christ is in you. The therapeutic substitute — affirming oneself rather than examining oneself — cannot perform this function, because it has no criterion outside the self to measure by. And Romans 12:2 shows where the capacity to prove comes from: not from cleverness but from a mind being renewed, which is why discernment grows with sanctification and not merely with study.
roots_summary: Hebrew nasah (H5254), to test, try, prove — the verb of Gen 22:1; bachan (H974), to examine as metal is assayed; Greek dokimazo (G1381), to test and thereby approve.
roots_lines: Hebrew nasah (H5254) — to test, prove, try; God proving Abraham (Gen 22:1) and Israel in the wilderness, to know what was in their heart (Deu 8:2).
Hebrew bachan (H974) — to examine, assay, as a refiner tests metal; examine me, O LORD, and prove me (Psa 26:2).
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test with a view to approving; prove all things (1Th 5:21), the root of dokimos, approved, and its negative adokimos, reprobate.
usage: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” — addressed to ordinary believers.
“That ye may prove what is that good… will of God” — discernment as a fruit of renewal.
“Prove me now herewith, saith the LORD” — the one invitation to test God.
